/-!
# Conjecture 3.34

by D. I. Moldavanskiĭ

(Well-known problem). The conjugacy problem for groups with a single defining relation.

That is: is the conjugacy problem solvable for every one-relator group
$G = \langle x_1, \dots, x_n \mid r \rangle$? For each such group, is there an algorithm
which, given two words $u, v$ in the letters $x_1^{\pm 1}, \dots, x_n^{\pm 1}$, decides
whether the elements of $G$ represented by $u$ and $v$ are conjugate in $G$?

*Reference:* [The Kourovka Notebook](https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v46)
-/

blocks.code:
@[category research open, AMS 3 20]
theorem kourovka.«3.34» : answer(sorry) ↔
    ∀ (n : ℕ) (r : FreeGroup (Fin n)),
      ComputablePred fun p : List (Fin n × Bool) × List (Fin n × Bool) =>
        IsConj (PresentedGroup.mk {r} (FreeGroup.mk p.1))
          (PresentedGroup.mk {r} (FreeGroup.mk p.2)) := by
  sorry
blocks.docstring:
(Well-known problem). Is the conjugacy problem solvable for every group with a single
defining relation?

That is, for every $n$ and every element $r$ of the free group on $x_1, \dots, x_n$, let
$G = \langle x_1, \dots, x_n \mid r \rangle$. Is the predicate on pairs $(u, v)$ of words over
the alphabet $x_1^{\pm 1}, \dots, x_n^{\pm 1}$ which holds exactly when the images of $u$ and
$v$ in $G$ are conjugate a computable predicate?

A word is a `List (Fin n × Bool)`, as in `FreeGroup.mk`: the letter `(i, true)` is $x_i$ and
`(i, false)` is $x_i^{-1}$. The decision procedure may depend on $n$ and $r$, i.e. the question
is asked for each one-relator group separately.

blocks.code:
@[category test, AMS 3 20]
theorem computablePred_isConj_of_fin_zero (r : FreeGroup (Fin 0)) :
    ComputablePred fun p : List (Fin 0 × Bool) × List (Fin 0 × Bool) =>
      IsConj (PresentedGroup.mk {r} (FreeGroup.mk p.1))
        (PresentedGroup.mk {r} (FreeGroup.mk p.2)) := by
  have h : ∀ p : List (Fin 0 × Bool) × List (Fin 0 × Bool),
      IsConj (PresentedGroup.mk {r} (FreeGroup.mk p.1))
        (PresentedGroup.mk {r} (FreeGroup.mk p.2)) := by
    intro p
    rw [Subsingleton.elim (FreeGroup.mk p.1) (FreeGroup.mk p.2)]
  exact ⟨fun p => isTrue (h p), by simpa [h] using Computable.const true⟩

claims.decomposer_note: Read as the standard yes/no question 'Is the conjugacy problem decidable (solvable) for every one-relator group ⟨x_1,…,x_n | r⟩?' — i.e. for each finitely generated group with a single defining relator, is the set of pairs of words over the generators representing conjugate elements a decidable (computable) predicate; the implicit quantifier is non-uniform (an algorithm for each such group, given its finite presentation), the generating set is implicitly finite, and the known partial results (e.g. Newman's solution for one-relator groups with torsion) are not part of the posed question, so no variants are added.
claims.reviewer_why: All eight candidates state the same non-uniform reading: for every n and relator r, the predicate on pairs of raw words List (Fin n × Bool) asserting conjugacy (IsConj) of their images in PresentedGroup {r} is ComputablePred. Verified against Mathlib source: ComputablePred = ∃ DecidablePred, Computable decide (algorithm may depend on n, r — matches the decomposition notes); PresentedGroup {r} = FreeGroup (Fin n) ⧸ normalClosure {r} is exactly the one-relator group; IsConj is ordinary group conjugacy. answer(True) states a positive answer for all one-relator groups, answer(False) a negative one. c08 chosen for its clear docstring, AMS 3 20 (computability + group theory, as in the repo's BranchingVAS precedent), and its n = 0 sanity test theorem; docstrings lightly edited and the test proof simplified. c01/c02/c07's `r : List (Fin n × Bool)` is equivalent (FreeGroup.mk surjective, quantifier non-uniform); c05's bespoke HasSolvableConjugacyProblem adds no clarity over the inline form.

import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Conjecture 3.34

by D. I. Moldavanskiĭ

(Well-known problem). The conjugacy problem for groups with a single defining relation.

That is: is the conjugacy problem solvable for every one-relator group
$G = \langle x_1, \dots, x_n \mid r \rangle$? For each such group, is there an algorithm
which, given two words $u, v$ in the letters $x_1^{\pm 1}, \dots, x_n^{\pm 1}$, decides
whether the elements of $G$ represented by $u$ and $v$ are conjugate in $G$?

*Reference:* [The Kourovka Notebook](https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v46)
-/

namespace Kourovka.«3.34»

/--
(Well-known problem). Is the conjugacy problem solvable for every group with a single
defining relation?

That is, for every $n$ and every element $r$ of the free group on $x_1, \dots, x_n$, let
$G = \langle x_1, \dots, x_n \mid r \rangle$. Is the predicate on pairs $(u, v)$ of words over
the alphabet $x_1^{\pm 1}, \dots, x_n^{\pm 1}$ which holds exactly when the images of $u$ and
$v$ in $G$ are conjugate a computable predicate?

A word is a `List (Fin n × Bool)`, as in `FreeGroup.mk`: the letter `(i, true)` is $x_i$ and
`(i, false)` is $x_i^{-1}$. The decision procedure may depend on $n$ and $r$, i.e. the question
is asked for each one-relator group separately.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 3 20]
theorem kourovka.«3.34» : answer(sorry) ↔
    ∀ (n : ℕ) (r : FreeGroup (Fin n)),
      ComputablePred fun p : List (Fin n × Bool) × List (Fin n × Bool) =>
        IsConj (PresentedGroup.mk {r} (FreeGroup.mk p.1))
          (PresentedGroup.mk {r} (FreeGroup.mk p.2)) := by
  sorry

/--
Sanity check of the formulation in the degenerate case of no generators: the group
$\langle \; \mid r \rangle$ is trivial, so any two words represent conjugate elements, and the
conjugacy predicate is computable.
-/
@[category test, AMS 3 20]
theorem computablePred_isConj_of_fin_zero (r : FreeGroup (Fin 0)) :
    ComputablePred fun p : List (Fin 0 × Bool) × List (Fin 0 × Bool) =>
      IsConj (PresentedGroup.mk {r} (FreeGroup.mk p.1))
        (PresentedGroup.mk {r} (FreeGroup.mk p.2)) := by
  have h : ∀ p : List (Fin 0 × Bool) × List (Fin 0 × Bool),
      IsConj (PresentedGroup.mk {r} (FreeGroup.mk p.1))
        (PresentedGroup.mk {r} (FreeGroup.mk p.2)) := by
    intro p
    rw [Subsingleton.elim (FreeGroup.mk p.1) (FreeGroup.mk p.2)]
  exact ⟨fun p => isTrue (h p), by simpa [h] using Computable.const true⟩

end Kourovka.«3.34»

items: Generators are indexed by `Fin n` for an arbitrary `n : ℕ` (implicitly finite generating set, as in the decomposition notes); every finitely generated one-relator group is isomorphic to one of this form.

Words are modelled as `List (Fin n × Bool)` (the raw word type of `FreeGroup.mk`, letter `(i, true)` = x_i, `(i, false)` = x_i⁻¹) rather than as elements of `FreeGroup (Fin n)`, because `ComputablePred` needs a `Primcodable` domain and Mathlib has no `Primcodable (FreeGroup α)` instance; lists over `Fin n × Bool` have the standard instance. This matches the informal 'pairs of words over the generators'.

The relator `r` ranges over all of `FreeGroup (Fin n)`, including `r = 1` (free group) and `n = 0` (trivial group); these degenerate presentations have decidable conjugacy problems, so including them does not change the truth value of the question. A `category test` theorem checks the `n = 0` case.
Conjugacy is `IsConj` in `PresentedGroup {r}`; for a group this is ordinary conjugacy (∃ c, c * a * c⁻¹ = b).
The decidability notion is Mathlib's `ComputablePred` (partial recursive functions on ℕ via `Primcodable` encodings), which is the standard formal counterpart of 'the conjugacy problem is solvable'.
AMS tags `3 20`: computability (03D40, word/conjugacy problems) and group theory (20F10).

reviewer_notes: The Kourovka statement is a bare title ('The conjugacy problem for groups with a single defining relation'); following the decomposition table it is read as 'is the conjugacy problem solvable for every finitely generated one-relator group ⟨x_1,…,x_n | r⟩?', non-uniformly. Degenerate cases n = 0 (trivial group) and r = 1 (free group) are included; both have decidable conjugacy so they do not change the truth value, and the n = 0 case is proved as a category test theorem. Words are raw signed words (List (Fin n × Bool)) because Mathlib has no Primcodable instance on FreeGroup; this matches the classical input format for decision problems. No candidate omitted the slot; no objections to the decomposition were raised. Final file compiles with only the 'declaration uses sorry' warning.
